title: Why We Need a Typical Value

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A measure of central tendency is a single value chosen to represent where a whole distribution is centred.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Chapter 1 turned a raw list of 30 weights into a frequency table (recall §1.4.1). If a colleague asks “how are the children in today’s clinic doing, weight-wise?”, you do not read out the table. You say one number: “the average weight was 11.8 kg.” That number answers “what is typical here?” and pays for its brevity by discarding all the individual variation. Chapter 3 recovers that variation.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Two blocks in a district survey report average birthweights of 2.9 kg and 3.1 kg. You compare them at a glance. Comparing two full frequency tables to reach the same conclusion is slow and error-prone, even though the tables hold strictly more information.

points.html: Three measures exist: mean, median and mode. Each answers “what is typical?” differently and suits different scales and shapes (§2.5).
Any single summary discards spread. Reporting a mean with no SD, or a median with no IQR, is a common and misleading shortcut (SD and IQR are defined in §3.7 and §3.4).
